title: Straw (6 December 1273)
hookLine: after an experience at Mass he stops writing: all I've written seems like straw

cards: A pen goes down on a desk and doesn't get picked up again. That's the whole scene. No fire, no vision on a mountain.
As tradition tells it, Thomas Aquinas, in the middle of the third part of the Summa, the great book this block has been walking through, goes to Mass one morning in Naples. Something happens there.
Afterward he stops writing, and he doesn't start again. His friends are alarmed. His companion Reginald keeps asking why.

teach.b: Tradition gives his answer like this. I can't, Reginald. Everything I have written seems to me like straw, compared with what I have seen.
In Latin the word is palea: straw, or chaff, the dry husk left when the grain is gone.
Nobody knows what Thomas saw. He didn't describe it, the people who passed the story down didn't claim to know, and it's better not to fill in the silence for him.
What tradition does say is that the Summa was left unfinished. One easy reading is that his work was worthless, and he finally admitted it. Catholics haven't taken it that way.
The Church went on to call him a Doctor of the Church and still teaches from his books. The point is the comparison.
A map is straw next to the mountain. A letter is straw next to the person walking through the door. Thomas had written that what we say of God is true, but always falls short of him.

Here he seems to have felt that falling short from the inside. Paul says something close, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Some readers notice one more thing.
It held the grain while it grew.

So Thomas's words may be straw, and still worth carrying. And there's a quiet lesson in the stopping: a mind that had hardly ever stopped set the pen down, and rested in something bigger than its work.

how: Catholics tell this story when speaking of Thomas, as a reminder that even the best theology falls short of God; the Summa itself is still studied in seminaries and universities.

games.q: you're Reginald. your friend Thomas has stopped writing in the middle of his great book. what do you do?
o: finish the book for him without asking.
games.why: Reginald keeps asking, and tradition gives Thomas's answer: everything I have written seems like straw, compared with what I have seen.

practice: Notice whatever task is pulling at you right now, the email, the dishes, the deadline, and let it sit on the desk for a little while; you'll pick it up again, though Thomas didn't.
Let your hands go loose, and let your work be smaller than you, just for this sit. If you pray, rest in God without saying anything at all.

wordCard.voice: Straw. In Latin, palea, the dry husk around the grain. Thomas's word, tradition says, for all he had written, next to what he had seen. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: straw, or chaff, the husk left when the grain is threshed out.

carryVoice: Your line: like straw. Words fall short of God, and can still be worth carrying. Until tomorrow.
